chain-of-responsibility.scenario: Support routes tickets by refund amount to an agent or supervisor.
chain-of-responsibility.request: Escalate large tickets to a manager without changing existing handlers.
chain-of-responsibility.problem: One routing function knows every level and changes whenever a handler is added.
chain-of-responsibility.solution: Each handler handles a request or forwards it to the next. The caller knows only the head. This example stops at the first match and defines an unhandled result; all-handler middleware is a different chain policy.
benefits: Insert a handler without editing existing classes.
Callers do not know the final receiver.
chain-of-responsibility.when: Use it when ordered candidates may handle a request.
chain-of-responsibility.avoid: Avoid it for a fixed receiver or untestable implicit ordering.
chain-of-responsibility.tradeoff: Requests may be unhandled; order matters. Prevent cycles and preserve tracing.
chain-of-responsibility.remember: Handle it if able; otherwise pass it on.

command.scenario: A toolbar edits text directly without retaining an undoable action.
command.request: Undo an inserted piece of text.
command.problem: Buttons are coupled to editing behavior, and undo needs a record of the previous state.
command.solution: Encapsulate insertion in a command holding its receiver, arguments and prior state. An invoker executes it and retains history for undo. The command represents a request; the editor performs the work.
benefits: Each action owns its undo information.
command.when: Use it for undo, histories, deferred work or queues.
command.avoid: Use a function for a simple immediate call without a request lifecycle.
command.tradeoff: History costs memory. External side effects may need compensation rather than true reversal.
command.remember: Retain what to do as an object, then decide when to execute or undo it.

interpreter.scenario: A rule engine checks age over 18 and later needs to combine that with membership.
interpreter.request: Represent age > 18 AND member as independently evaluated expressions.
interpreter.problem: Ad hoc string handling tangles grammar with evaluation. Evaluating arbitrary code is unsafe.
interpreter.solution: Represent grammar with expression objects. Terminals read context; nonterminals combine child expressions through interpret(context). This example constructs an AST directly, not a complete parser.
benefits: Make grammar explicit without executing arbitrary code.
Extend a small grammar through composition.
interpreter.when: Use it for a small, stable rule language.
interpreter.avoid: Use maintained parsers, compilers or rule engines for complex or performance-critical languages.
interpreter.tradeoff: Grammar classes proliferate, and parsing, diagnostics and safety limits still need implementation.
interpreter.remember: Turn a rule into a recursively evaluated expression tree.

iterator.scenario: A playlist stores songs in an array and callers access its indices.
iterator.request: Offer forward and reverse traversal without exposing the array.
iterator.problem: Callers depend on storage layout, so changing representation or order changes their loops.
iterator.solution: Let the collection return an iterator that owns a cursor and implements next. Use the language's iterator protocol. Forward and reverse iterators share the collection but maintain independent traversal state.
iterator.when: Use it for multiple traversals or hidden collection storage.
iterator.avoid: Use built-in collection iterators when they already meet the need.
iterator.tradeoff: Define mutation behavior during iteration; this example uses a sequence snapshot.
iterator.remember: The collection owns data; the iterator owns where traversal has reached.

mediator.scenario: A search box updates results directly, while a clear button accesses both the box and results.
mediator.request: Coordinate search and clear without direct widget references.
mediator.problem: Widgets know each other, so new interaction rules require edits across components.
mediator.solution: Widgets report events to a mediator. The mediator knows coordination rules and updates the appropriate widgets; widgets no longer control each other.
benefits: Centralize the effect of an interaction.
Reuse widgets in other coordination contexts.
mediator.when: Use it for dense interactions governed by a shared workflow.
mediator.avoid: Skip it for a simple one-way dependency and avoid one application-wide god mediator.
mediator.tradeoff: Mediators can grow large; split them by collaboration scope.
mediator.remember: Components report events; the mediator coordinates responses.

memento.scenario: An editor holds text and selection, and an external history wants undo snapshots.
memento.request: Save, keep editing, then restore both text and selection.
memento.problem: Copying private fields exposes internals and makes history depend on the editor's layout.
memento.solution: The editor creates and restores an immutable snapshot; history only retains it. Memento stores state rather than actions. TypeScript hides state in a closure; Python uses a frozen value with an opaque-state convention.
benefits: History does not depend on editor fields.
memento.when: Use it to restore state without exposing internal representation.
memento.avoid: For huge or noncopyable state, consider incremental logs or persistent structures.
memento.tradeoff: Snapshots cost memory and need version and restore-access policies.
memento.remember: The object packages and restores its state; history only keeps it.

observer.scenario: An inventory service directly refreshes a display when stock changes.
observer.request: Notify email alerts and the display, with unsubscribe support.
observer.problem: The publisher knows each consumer, so additions and removals change publishing logic.
observer.solution: A publisher retains callbacks and notifies a snapshot after state changes. Consumers subscribe and unsubscribe themselves. This example is synchronous in-process notification, not a durable queue.
benefits: The publisher is independent of concrete consumers.
observer.when: Use it when one object's changes should notify multiple dynamically registered consumers.
observer.avoid: Use mature messaging infrastructure for durable delivery, retries or cross-process events.
observer.tradeoff: Manage unsubscribe, failures, notification loops and ordering; this example does not guarantee reliable delivery.
observer.remember: Subscribe to changes without making the publisher know every consumer.

state.scenario: A player interprets the same click differently when stopped or playing.
state.request: Add a paused state and resume on click.
state.problem: State branches accumulate in the player and affect more operations as states grow.
state.solution: The player delegates to its current state object. Stopped, Playing and Paused define click and transition the context according to business rules. State includes transitions, not just interchangeable algorithms.
benefits: Remove accumulating state branches from the context.
state.when: Use it when behavior depends on state and the state/operation set is growing.
state.avoid: For a few stable states, an enum and switch may be clearer. Use a maintained state-machine library for complex workflows.
state.tradeoff: More classes can scatter transitions. Define illegal transitions and concurrency policies.
state.remember: The current state determines an action's meaning and the next state.

template-method.scenario: CSV and JSON imports duplicate read, transform and save steps.
template-method.request: Keep read and save fixed while changing format-specific transformation.
template-method.problem: Copied workflows drift in ordering and shared behavior.
template-method.solution: A base importData fixes the read-transform-save skeleton and invokes an abstract transformation step. CSV and JSON subclasses implement that step. The example follows this convention without language-enforced final methods.
template-method.when: Use it for similar workflows with a few varying steps and a natural inheritance relationship.
template-method.avoid: Prefer composition or strategy for freely interchangeable runtime behaviors.
template-method.tradeoff: Subclasses depend on the base workflow contract; too many hooks obscure it.
template-method.remember: The base owns the skeleton; subclasses supply the varying steps.

visitor.scenario: A filesystem contains files and folders. It needs size calculation and later a name export.
visitor.request: Add export without adding another method to every node class.
visitor.problem: Every new operation edits all element classes, mixing structure with unrelated algorithms.
visitor.solution: Elements accept a visitor and invoke visitFile or visitFolder with themselves. The visitor implements type-specific operations through double dispatch and owns folder recursion. New operations add visitors; new element types change every visitor.
benefits: Keep an operation together in one visitor.
Add operations to a stable element structure.
Dispatch by element type without caller-side type checks.
visitor.when: Use it when element types are stable and operations keep growing.
visitor.avoid: Avoid it when element types grow frequently; pattern matching may be clearer in some languages.
visitor.tradeoff: Visitors know every element type and may need access to element state.
visitor.remember: Bring a new operation to the structure rather than adding it to every element.
